title: Love and Duty
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 39 of 40
content:
The message arrived during our first real dinner in the rebuilt house.

Of course it did.

A young Air Acolyte stood at the courtyard gate soaked in rain, holding a sealed dispatch from the western district.

A spirit had appeared near a rail excavation.

Workers were missing.

The local magistrate requested the Avatar immediately.

Aang read the message once.

Then again.

Nobody spoke.

The old pattern stood up in the room with us.

Aang leaves.

We understand.

The world needs him.

Dinner cools.

Love becomes the quiet thing waiting after duty finishes.

Aang folded the dispatch.

“How long?” Katara asked.

The Acolyte shook his head. “We don’t know. The rail camp is two hours by bison.”

Aang looked toward the table.

Four bowls.

Steam still rising.

Toph’s foot pressed into the floor.

I felt anger begin before I wanted it.

Not at the missing workers.

At timing. At history. At the unfairness of loving someone whose responsibility could walk through the gate at any moment wearing wet clothes.

Aang looked at us.

“I have to go.”

“Yes,” Katara said.

Toph’s jaw tightened.

“Yes,” I said.

Aang closed his eyes for half a second.

Then he turned to the Acolyte.

“Go tell the magistrate I’m coming. Ask the school to prepare Appa, emergency supplies, and two spirit-response teams.”

The Acolyte bowed and ran.

Aang did not move.

Toph tilted her head.

“Well?”

“I have ten minutes.”

The sentence changed everything.

Not much.

Ten minutes did not solve the conflict.

But old Aang would already have been gone.

Katara’s expression softened.

“Eat.”

He sat.

We ate quickly.

Not pretending the message had not arrived.

Aang explained what he knew. I pulled a regional map from the office. Toph identified the excavation geology from survey records she had reviewed months earlier. Katara packed medical supplies for him to take.

Home did not compete with duty.

It prepared him for it.

At the gate, Aang kissed Katara.

Toph.

Me.

Then he stopped.

“Come with me?”

All three of us stared.

Aang laughed nervously. “Not because I’m volunteering you. I’m asking.”

Toph’s mouth twitched.

“What do you need?” Katara asked.

“Toph knows the ground. You know field medicine. Paperwork knows the rail contracts and worker camps.”

He looked at each of us.

“But no is allowed.”

There it was.

The repair turned into practice.

Katara said yes.

Toph said, “Obviously.”

I said yes after checking the council emergency rota and assigning my morning work to someone else.

Progress looked ridiculous sometimes.

We left together.

The rail camp had cut too close to an ancient hot spring sacred to a local spirit.

Not maliciously.

Ignorantly.

Survey maps marked the spring as geothermal runoff. Workers had driven steel pilings through the stone chamber beneath it.

The spirit responded by filling the excavation with dense white fog and leading anyone who entered in circles until they collapsed from exhaustion.

Fourteen workers were missing.

Aang did not attack the spirit.

Of course he did not.

He sat at the edge of the fog and listened.

That looked like doing nothing to several terrified supervisors.

Toph nearly punched one when he said so.

Katara set up a treatment station.

I pulled contracts.

The rail company had been warned about the spring by three local families and ignored them because the objections had not been filed through the central survey office.

Paperwork again.

A mechanism for accountability.

A weapon when used to dismiss knowledge that arrived in the wrong format.

I felt sick.

Toph placed both hands on the ground.

“The chamber’s cracking,” she said. “If they pull the pilings wrong, it collapses.”

Aang opened his eyes.

“The spirit is protecting it.”

A supervisor snapped, “The spirit trapped fourteen people!”

Aang stood.

“Yes.”

His voice was calm.

“And your company drove steel through its home after local residents told you not to.”

The man’s mouth closed.

Aang looked toward the fog.

“Both things can be wrong.”

That became our task.

Not choosing one innocent side.

Getting people out while repairing what people had damaged.

Toph mapped the underground chamber through vibration. Aang entered the fog with a line tied around his waist—not because he needed restraint, but because the others did. Katara moved along the perimeter, using water from the spring to mark safe paths where the spirit allowed passage.

I stood beside local residents and wrote down the names the company had ignored.

One woman, old enough that her hands shook, told me the spring had been protected for six generations.

“We said it.”

“I know.”

“No. You know now.”

The words struck like Toph.

I wrote them exactly.

All fourteen workers came out alive.

The last one emerged leaning on Aang just before dawn.

The spirit appeared then.

Not fully human. Not animal. A shape of steam, antlers, water, and light rising over the shattered spring.

Everyone backed away except Aang.

Toph remained beside him because of course she did.

Katara stood on his other side.

I stayed where I was.

Some moments belonged to people who could speak the world’s older languages.

Aang bowed.

He promised the pilings would be removed.

The company supervisor started to object.

I handed him the contract clause allowing emergency rerouting where construction endangered protected cultural sites.

He stared.

I smiled.

Paperwork could have a dramatic entrance occasionally.

The spirit dissolved into rain.

The supervisor tried to leave before the workers could give their statements. One of the women whose family had warned about the spring stepped directly into his path.

"Your forms told us we weren't qualified to know where the water went," she said. "Now you want our names on a report saying you fixed it?"

"We have to notify the central office."

"Then notify them we warned you."

I had a ledger and a box of damp pencils. I asked the workers to tell me what they had seen, not what the company had instructed them to say. Several were frightened about losing shifts if they contradicted the foreman. The woman from the spring offered her front room as a place for them to speak together, with a witness of their choosing.

Aang had just bowed to a spirit. He was exhausted and streaked with mud. He could have given a beautiful speech that settled nothing. Instead, he turned to the supervisor.

"Work stays stopped until the spring and pilings are independently assessed," he said. "The workers' wages don't stop because the company made an unsafe choice."

Katara looked up from binding a miner's wrist. "And the injury reports go to the healers, not only the people who caused the injuries."

Toph tested the ground beyond the rail tie. "Nobody moves that beam until somebody's checked the chamber underneath it. And if somebody says the ground's fine because they're wearing a fancy hat, send them to me."

The supervisor didn't look pleased. The workers did not cheer. They started writing their own names on a page that would be copied to more than one office, because one forgotten complaint was how this had begun.

I stood back to let the woman from the spring read the final line before we sent it. She corrected the name of the old path. We changed it. It mattered that the document sounded like the people who had lived there.

By sunrise, the fog thinned.

We sat on a rail tie eating cold buns from the emergency pack.

Aang looked exhausted.

Toph leaned against his shoulder.

Katara’s hair had escaped every tie.

I had mud inside one boot.

“This was our first dinner,” I said.

Aang winced.

“Technically we ate it.”

“Fast.”

“Together.”

Toph pointed a bun at him. “Don’t get sentimental. I haven’t slept.”

Katara rested her head against my shoulder.

“Love and duty,” she said.

Aang looked toward the spring.

“I keep acting like they’re opposite directions.”

“Sometimes they are,” I said.

He turned toward me.

“If duty always wins,” I continued, “love becomes the thing that pays for it.”

Aang was quiet.

“And if love always wins,” Katara added, “you stop being who you are.”

Toph chewed her bun.

“So stop making everything a contest.”

We looked at her.

She shrugged.

“Sometimes you leave. Sometimes we come. Sometimes we say no. Sometimes the world waits ten minutes while you finish dinner.”

Aang smiled.

“That’s annoyingly wise.”

“I’m surrounded by idiots. Somebody has to do it.”

The sun rose over the rail camp.

Workers began dismantling the first section of track.

Local families stood with engineers, marking a new route.

Not harmony.

Work.

I leaned against the people I loved.

Duty was not proof that love mattered less.

Love was not an exemption from duty.

The question was whether either became an excuse to stop choosing.

That morning, tired and muddy beside a wounded spring, we chose again.

We returned from the spring three days later smelling like wet stone and medicinal herbs.

The first thing Toph said when she opened the door was, “You both stink.”

The second was, “You’re late.”

The third never became words.

She caught Aang by the front of his robe and pulled him into a hug hard enough to make him wheeze.

Katara embraced me at the same time, one hand settling at the back of my neck.

No one pretended we had not been afraid.

Dinner that night was leftovers reheated badly because none of us wanted to spend another hour apart in different rooms.

Aang told us about the injured spirit spring between bites. Katara corrected his medical details. I explained the negotiations with the nearby village. Toph interrupted to demand why neither of us had sent a messenger sooner.

“We were busy.”

“Bad answer.”

“It’s the true one.”

“Still bad.”

Aang reached across the table. “You’re right.”

Toph went quiet.

That was one of the hardest lessons duty kept teaching us: being needed elsewhere did not erase the effect of disappearing here.

We could have valid reasons and still owe one another repair.

“I’m sorry,” I said. “Next time, information becomes part of the emergency plan.”

Katara nodded. “Yes.”

Toph stabbed a vegetable with unnecessary force. “Good.”

Aang looked around the table.

“Love and duty,” he said.

“Don’t make it a slogan,” Toph warned.

“It could be a very nice banner.”

“I will burn it.”

“You’re not a firebender.”

“I know people.”

We laughed.

The choice renewed itself in the argument.

The next time duty called, we did better. Not perfectly. A messenger went out before we left. Katara wrote the destination. Aang added the expected return. I wrote what we knew and what we did not.

Toph later complained that our handwriting was terrible.

She also kept the message pinned beside the door until we came home.

Love had not made duty smaller. It had made communication part of doing duty well.

We added the messenger rule to our household agreement that night. Toph complained about bureaucracy in romance while insisting the wording be precise.

That contradiction felt exactly like us.
